2. WHITE HOUSE REGULATORY OVERSIGHT 
FROM NIXON TO BIDEN
In stark contrast with the foregoing, no institutional development in 
U.S. administrative law over the last several decades has been more 
notable than the routinization of White House oversight of regulatory- 
policy making. In particular, each president from Richard Nixon through 
Donald Trump not only asserted presidential authority to guide the 
exercise of administrative discretion, but attempted, with increasing 
ambition, to systematize the president’s capacity to oversee and coordinate 
policy making within the executive branch. From the Reagan 
Administration on, the systemization of such oversight has occurred 
largely pursuant to the terms of formal executive orders, which purport to 
rest on inherent powers of presidential information-seeking, coordination, 
and supervision conferred by Article H. These efforts highlight a 
competition among administrative law values that may defy RimnIf.Aneons 
optimization: political responsiveness, instrumental rationality, public 
transparency, government efficiency, and legal accountability.
Going beyond the efforts of Presidents Nixon, Ford, and Carter to 
promote various forms of non-binding rulemaking analysis and 
interagency consultation on regulatory policy. President Reagan issued an 
executive order within a month of taking office that imposed detailed 
responsibilities on OMB for managing the process of producing and 
reviewing regulatory impact analyses emanating from the agencies. Exec. 
Order No. 12,291, 40 Fed. Reg. 13193 (1981). The order articulated a set of 
overarching executive branch policy mandates with respect to 
administrative rulemaking, and, unlike earher presidential orders, 
required executive agency heads, to the extent permitted by statute, to be 
guided by both 12,291’s stated policy goals and its procedural requirements 
in the exercise of administrative discretion. These provisions—and the 
designation of OMB as a central authority for reviewing significant 
rulemaking proposals across the board—amounted to a striking and 
controversial transformation of federal regulatory process. On the history 
behind the Reagan order and the poHtical and academic controversies that 
ensued, see Ashraf Ahmed, Lev Menand, and Noah Rosenblum, The 
Making of Presidential Administration, 137 Ha r v . L. Re v . 2131, 2153- 
2173 (2024).
President George H.W. Bush left the Reagan process formally in tn ct 
while also vesting further oversight responsibihty in the President’s 
Council on Competitiveness, chaired by Vice President Quayle. Although 
composed of the Administration’s major economic advisers, the Council 
functioned chiefly through the vice president’s staff as a source of pressure 
on OMB and other agencies, especially EPA, to take account of economic 
impacts in the course of regulatory pohcy making. See Kirk Victor, Quayle's 
Quiet Coup, Na t ’L J., July 6, 1991, at 1676.
